title: Saying It Precisely
overview: Describe something so exactly that nobody has to ask a second question. Build adjectives out of two words, choose between an -ing and an -ed adjective, and say how big a difference is rather than just that there is one. Start a sentence with an activity, and use the prepositions that name a state: in charge, under pressure, out of work.
learningPath: The lesson: listen first, then read it back.
Words: five groups, 29 words. Listen and say each one.
Patterns: 5 cards. Read the one done for you before you try.
Reading: an auction catalogue, a language guide and a returns form.
Speaking: tap the mic, say it, listen back.
Writing: four tasks, each with a model.
Practice and the check: 7 exercises, then 12 questions.
functions: Describe an object so precisely that nobody needs to ask again
Say how big a difference is, not only that there is one
Describe a job as demanding, rewarding or challenging
Start a sentence with an activity: learning, waiting, getting there early
Say that somebody is in charge, under pressure or out of work
Ask a question that gets a fact rather than an opinion
Sum up what somebody else has just said
lectureScript:
This unit is about being exact.
Not about using longer words, and not about being polite. About saying a thing so clearly that the person listening does not have to ask again.
That matters in a shop, in a complaint, on a form, and in any job where somebody acts on what you wrote.

Start with a warning about one word.
Lovely. Also nice, great, terrible and horrible.
Those words tell somebody what you think. They tell them nothing about the thing.
If you say the table is lovely, nobody knows how big it is, what it is made of, or what condition it is in.
The reading in this unit is an auction catalogue, and catalogues are written by people who are not allowed to say lovely.
Watch what they do instead.

The first pattern is a way of building new adjectives, and English does this constantly.
You take two words and join them with a hyphen, and the pair goes in front of a noun.
A well-made chair. A three-year contract. A hand-written label. A part-time job.
There is one rule that catches everybody, and it is worth hearing twice.
The noun in the middle stays singular.
A three-year contract, not a three-years contract.
A ten-minute walk, not a ten-minutes walk.
The number has already told the listener it is more than one, so the noun does not repeat the message.
And the hyphen only appears in front of a noun. Move the words after the noun and it comes apart: the chair is well made.

The second pattern is an increment on something you already have.
Level 2 gave you the pair: the film was boring, and I was bored.
That rule is correct, and it covers less than half of these words.
A great many participle adjectives have no partner that anybody actually says.
A demanding job, but nobody says a demanded job.
Rewarding work, but nobody says rewarded work.
And it runs the other way too. An experienced driver. A qualified electrician. The people involved.
None of those has an everyday -ing half.
So the question to ask is still the same one. What does the thing DO, or how is the person?
But when you have never heard the other half of the pair, assume it is not there.

The third pattern is about the size of a difference.
In Level 2 you learned far better and much worse, and here that becomes a system.
In front of a comparative you can put much, far, a lot, slightly, considerably.
What you can never put there is very.
Very cheap is fine. Very cheaper is not English.
And there is a second way to do the same job, which is as good as.
It is as good as the other one means they are the same.
It is not as good as the other one means it is worse, and it says so far more gently.
That gentleness is the reason to learn it. In a complaint, in a review, in anything you might have to defend, not as good as is easier to stand behind than worse.

The fourth pattern moves something you already own into a new position.
You can already say I enjoy walking and she stopped eating: the -ing form after a verb.
Now put it at the FRONT, where it becomes the subject of the sentence.
Learning a language takes years.
Waiting is the hardest part.
Getting there early made all the difference.
There is one trap, and it catches almost everybody.
Learning languages TAKES years. Not take.
The subject is the activity, and an activity is one thing, however many nouns come after it.

The fifth pattern is a set of prepositions that go in front of a noun.
Level 2 gave you fixed phrases to memorise whole: by bus, in cash, at once.
These are different, because the preposition is carrying a meaning you can reuse.
In means inside a state or a role: in charge, in favour of, in writing.
Under means a force pressing on you: under pressure, under review, under repair.
At means a point, often a point of danger: at risk, at fault, at short notice.
Out of means away from a state: out of order, out of stock, out of work.
Almost none of them takes an article, and adding one changes the meaning.
She is in charge of the team means she runs it.
She is in the charge of the team would mean they look after her.

Last, the words.
One group is adjectives that cannot be made stronger: freezing, boiling, exhausted, impossible, perfect, essential.
Each of those already sits at the end of a scale, so very has nothing left to do.
You use absolutely, completely, utterly or totally instead.
There is a quick test. If you can say slightly, the word is on a scale.
Slightly cold works, so cold takes very.
Slightly freezing does not work, so freezing takes absolutely.
Start with the words. Say each one aloud before you move on.

words.meaning: Extremely impressive or attractive.
words.example: The view from the top was stunning.
practice: She did a stunning job on the repair.
Stunning already means very impressive, so never say very stunning.
Stunning tells somebody what you think, not what the thing is like.
A catalogue will not write stunning, for exactly that reason.
words.tutor: Describe something stunning, then describe the same thing factually. Ask the tutor which was more useful.

words.meaning: Extremely large.
words.example: They moved into an enormous old house.
practice: The difference in price was enormous.
An enormous amount of work went into it.
Enormous is size, so it comes after an opinion word.
A lovely enormous garden, not an enormous lovely garden.
words.tutor: Describe something enormous. Ask the tutor where the size word sat.

words.meaning: Extremely small.
words.example: She wrote the note in tiny letters.
practice: The flat had a tiny kitchen and no window.
A tiny difference can still matter.
Tiny is the opposite end of the same scale as enormous.
Both tiny and enormous are already extreme: no very.
words.tutor: Describe something tiny. Ask the tutor to check the adjective order.

words.meaning: Very great in size or amount, usually of space or quantity.
words.example: A vast amount of data is collected every day.
practice: The vast majority of people never complain.
Vast suits space and quantity better than objects.
You would say a vast plain, but rarely a vast cup.
The vast difference in cost decided it.
words.tutor: Use vast about an amount, not an object. Ask the tutor whether it sounded natural.

words.meaning: Very small in degree; only just noticeable.
words.example: There was a slight delay on the line.
practice: A slight improvement is still an improvement.
She had a slight accent I could not place.
Slight is about degree, tiny is about size.
A slight change in the wording fixed it.
words.tutor: Describe a slight difference. Ask the tutor whether slight or tiny was right.

words.meaning: Large enough to matter; a good deal of something.
words.example: There was a considerable difference in price.
practice: It took a considerable amount of work.
Considerable is the formal word for a lot of.
Its adverb is considerably: considerably cheaper.
Considerable is the opposite of slight on the same scale.
words.tutor: Describe a considerable difference. Ask the tutor to check it was not a tiny one.

words.meaning: In the shape of an egg or a flattened circle.
words.example: The table was oval and far too big.
practice: An oval track is longer than it looks.
Oval is shape, so it follows size: a large oval table.
Oval is not the same as round: it is longer one way.
Oval is also a noun: they met on the oval.
words.tutor: Describe something oval. Ask the tutor where shape sits in the order.

words.meaning: In the shape of a rectangle.
words.example: Each panel is rectangular and identical.
practice: The rectangular window let in very little light.
Most doors are rectangular, so nobody says so.
Rectangular is precise; oblong is the older word.
A small rectangular metal box.
words.tutor: Describe something rectangular. Ask the tutor to check the order against shape.

words.meaning: Very old; belonging to the distant past.
words.example: They found an ancient wall under the car park.
practice: My ancient laptop still works, somehow.
Ancient is often used humorously about a thing that merely feels old.
Age follows shape: a round ancient table.
Ancient is already extreme, so no very.
words.tutor: Describe something ancient, seriously or humorously. Ask the tutor which reading came across.

words.meaning: Of the present or recent times.
words.example: The building is modern and badly insulated.
practice: Modern methods are not always better methods.
A modern flat can be smaller than an old one.
Modern is age, so it sits between shape and colour.
A small square modern white box.
words.tutor: Describe something modern. Ask the tutor to check where age sat.

words.meaning: Light in colour, with little strength of shade.
words.example: The walls were a pale grey.
practice: He looked pale after the journey.
A pale blue shirt shows every mark.
Pale goes before the colour it weakens: pale green.
Pale is the opposite of deep or rich for a colour.
words.tutor: Describe a pale colour. Ask the tutor to check pale came first.

words.meaning: Very bright and strong in colour; or very clear in the mind.
words.example: The walls were a vivid green.
practice: A vivid blue is the opposite of a pale one.
Vivid also describes a memory: a vivid recollection.
Vivid goes before the colour it strengthens: vivid red.
Pale and vivid are the two ends of the same scale.
words.tutor: Describe a vivid colour, then a pale one. Ask the tutor to check both.

words.meaning: Made of wood.
words.example: A long wooden bench ran along the wall.
practice: The wooden floor creaked in two places.
Material comes last, right before the noun.
A lovely old wooden chair, in that order.
Wooden can also mean stiff: a wooden performance.
words.tutor: Describe something wooden with two adjectives in front. Ask the tutor about the order.

words.meaning: Made of metal.
words.example: They replaced it with a metal frame.
practice: A small metal box sat on the shelf.
Metal is the material word; metallic means like metal.
Material sits closest to the noun of all of them.
A large square metal tray.
words.tutor: Describe something metal. Ask the tutor whether metal or metallic was right.

words.meaning: Made of plastic.
words.example: The handle is plastic and it will break.
practice: A cheap plastic chair is still a chair.
Plastic often carries a sense of poor quality.
Material last: a dreadful old plastic chair.
Plastic is also a noun: made of plastic.
words.tutor: Describe something plastic. Ask the tutor whether it sounded critical.

words.meaning: Made of wool.
words.example: She wore a heavy woollen coat all winter.
practice: A woollen blanket is warmer than it looks.
Woollen is the material; woolly means like wool.
A fine old woollen jacket.
Note the double l in woollen.
words.tutor: Describe something woollen. Ask the tutor to check the spelling.

words.meaning: Brought in from another country.
words.example: The imported parts cost twice as much.
practice: Imported goods take longer to replace.
Origin goes before material: an imported metal frame.
Imported is also a past participle: they imported it.
The imported model had a different plug.
words.tutor: Describe something imported. Ask the tutor where origin sat in the order.

words.meaning: From the area where you are.
words.example: We used local timber for the whole job.
practice: The local shop closes at six.
Local is the plain opposite of imported.
A good local builder is worth waiting for.
Local can also be a noun: he is a local.
words.tutor: Describe something local. Ask the tutor whether local was doing real work in the sentence.

groups.title: Adjectives that cannot be made stronger

words.meaning: Extremely cold. It is already the end of the scale.
words.example: The flat was freezing all February.
practice: It is freezing out there; take a coat.
Never very freezing. Say absolutely freezing.
Cold has degrees. Freezing does not.
Freezing is also the verb: the pipes are freezing.
words.tutor: Say something was freezing, with a degree word. Ask the tutor whether you avoided very.

words.meaning: Extremely hot. It is already the end of the scale.
words.example: The kitchen was boiling by two o'clock.
practice: It was absolutely boiling in there.
Never very boiling. Absolutely or completely.
Boiling and freezing sit at the two ends.
Boiling hot is common in speech, though it repeats itself.
words.tutor: Say something was boiling. Ask the tutor which degree word you used.

words.meaning: Extremely tired, with nothing left.
words.example: I was exhausted by the end of the shift.
practice: She was absolutely exhausted and said so.
Tired has degrees. Exhausted does not.
Never very exhausted. Completely exhausted.
Exhausted is a participle adjective, from exhaust.
words.tutor: Say when you were exhausted. Ask the tutor to check the degree word.

words.meaning: Not able to happen at all.
words.example: Finishing by Friday was impossible.
practice: It is absolutely impossible to park here.
Difficult has degrees. Impossible does not.
Never very impossible. Utterly or absolutely.
Impossible can describe a person: he is impossible.
words.tutor: Say something that was impossible. Ask the tutor whether you used a degree word that fits.

words.meaning: Extremely angry. It is already the end of the scale.
words.example: She was furious when she saw the invoice.
practice: He was absolutely furious about the delay.
Angry has degrees. Furious does not.
Never very furious. Absolutely furious.
Furious can also describe a pace: a furious rate of work.
words.tutor: Say when you were furious. Ask the tutor to check the degree word.

words.meaning: Extremely pleased. It is already the end of the scale.
words.example: They were delighted with the result.
practice: I was absolutely delighted to hear it.
Pleased has degrees. Delighted does not.
Never very delighted. Absolutely delighted.
Delighted takes with for a thing and to before a verb.
words.tutor: Say when you were delighted. Ask the tutor whether you used with or to correctly.

words.meaning: Completely; the degree word for an adjective with no scale.
words.example: The room was absolutely freezing.
practice: I was absolutely exhausted by six.
Absolutely goes with freezing, not with cold.
Very goes the other way: very cold, never very freezing.
Absolutely on its own means yes, completely.
words.tutor: Use absolutely with an adjective that has no scale. Ask the tutor whether the pair fits.

words.meaning: Entirely, with nothing left out.
words.example: The plan was completely impossible.
practice: She was completely exhausted after the drive.
Completely works with the same adjectives as absolutely.
Completely different, completely wrong, completely full.
Not completely means partly, which is different from not at all.
words.tutor: Use completely with an extreme adjective. Ask the tutor to check the pairing.

words.meaning: Completely, usually about something bad.
words.example: The instructions were utterly useless.
practice: I was utterly exhausted and could not think.
Utterly leans negative: utterly dreadful, rarely utterly perfect.
It is stronger and more formal than completely.
Utterly is the adverb from utter, which is also an adjective.
words.tutor: Use utterly about something bad. Ask the tutor whether it sounded too strong.

words.meaning: Completely, with no part left out.
words.example: The first attempt was entirely wrong.
practice: That is entirely my fault.
Entirely is slightly more formal than completely.
It pairs with the same extreme adjectives.
Not entirely means partly, which is not the same as not at all.
words.tutor: Use entirely with an extreme adjective. Ask the tutor whether it suited the register.

words.meaning: To a small degree. It goes with the adjectives that DO have a scale.
words.example: The second one was slightly cheaper.
practice: I was slightly tired, not exhausted.
Slightly goes with cold, tired, difficult. Never with freezing.
It is the opposite end from absolutely.
Slightly is the adverb from slight.
words.tutor: Use slightly with an adjective that has a scale. Ask the tutor to check the pairing.

grammar.title: A well-made chair, a three-year contract: adjectives built from two words
grammar.explanation:
English builds new adjectives by joining two words with a hyphen.
The pair sits in front of a noun and behaves as one adjective.
a well-made chair, a three-year contract, a part-time job
grammar.rule:
The commonest shapes:

adverb + participle   a well-made chair, a badly-written note
number + noun         a three-year contract, a ten-minute walk
noun + participle     a hand-written label, a home-made cake
adjective + noun      a full-time job, a long-term plan

The noun in the middle stays SINGULAR:
a three-year contract, NOT a three-years contract
a ten-minute walk, NOT a ten-minutes walk

The hyphen appears only in front of the noun:
a well-made chair  ->  the chair is well made
a part-time job    ->  she works part time
grammar.workedExample:
One done, step by step.
Make one adjective from this: a walk that takes ten minutes.
1. The two words are ten and minute.
2. Number plus noun, so the noun goes singular: ten-minute.
3. Join them with a hyphen and put them in front.
Answer: a ten-minute walk.
After the noun it comes apart again: the walk takes ten minutes.
grammar.mistake:
The plural is the error everybody makes.
No: a five-years plan.
Yes: a five-year plan.
The number already tells you it is more than one.
grammar.tip: Two words, one hyphen, in front of the noun. Singular in the middle.
grammar.practice:
Make one compound adjective for each.
1. A contract that lasts three years.  a ___ contract
2. A chair that was made well.  a ___ chair
3. A label that was written by hand.  a ___ label
4. A job that takes the full week.  a ___ job
5. A journey of forty minutes.  a ___ journey
6. A plan for the long term.  a ___ plan
Now put two of them after the noun instead.
7. The chair was ___ .
8. She works ___ .
grammar.answers:
1. three-year  2. well-made  3. hand-written  4. full-time
5. forty-minute  6. long-term
7. well made  8. part time, or full time
Numbers 7 and 8 lose the hyphen, because they no longer sit in front of a noun.
Wrong on 1 or 5? The noun in the middle never takes an s.
6 or more right: good.

grammar.title: Concerned, demanding, rewarding: the participle adjectives with no obvious pair
grammar.explanation:
Level 2 gave you the pairs: the work is boring, and I am bored.
That pattern is real, and it covers only part of the set.
Many participle adjectives have no partner in everyday use, and you meet
them one at a time: demanding, rewarding, concerned, involved.
grammar.rule:
The pairs you already have:
-ing = what the thing does.  The film was boring.
-ed  = how the person feels. I was bored.

The ones with no everyday partner:
demanding   a demanding job        (nobody says a demanded job)
rewarding   rewarding work         (nobody says rewarded work)
challenging a challenging year
convincing  a convincing argument

And the -ed ones that stand alone:
concerned   a concerned neighbour
involved    the people involved
experienced an experienced driver
qualified   a qualified electrician

involved changes meaning with position:
an involved explanation  = a complicated one
the people involved      = the people taking part
grammar.workedExample:
One done, step by step.
Choose: The work is hard, but it gives you a lot back. It is ___ .
1. Ask what the WORK does, not how you feel.
2. What the thing does takes -ing.
3. Giving a lot back is rewarding.
Answer: It is rewarding.
There is no everyday rewarded to pair it with, so the choice is not a pair here.
grammar.mistake:
Reaching for the missing half of a pair produces English nobody says.
No: It was a demanded job.
Yes: It was a demanding job.
When you have not heard the other half, assume it does not exist.
grammar.tip: Ask what the thing DOES for -ing, and how the person IS for -ed.
grammar.practice:
Choose the right form.
1. The job is hard and never stops. It is very (demanding / demanded).
2. She is an (experiencing / experienced) driver.
3. The argument was (convincing / convinced).
4. A (concerning / concerned) neighbour rang the council.
5. The work is hard but (rewarding / rewarded).
6. Everybody (involving / involved) was paid late.
7. He is a (qualifying / qualified) electrician.
8. It was a (challenging / challenged) year.
grammar.answers:
1. demanding  2. experienced  3. convincing  4. concerned
5. rewarding  6. involved  7. qualified  8. challenging
Numbers 1, 3, 5 and 8 describe what the thing does.
Numbers 2, 4, 6 and 7 describe the person, and none of them has an everyday -ing partner.
6 or more right: good.

grammar.title: Not as good as, much better than: putting a degree on a comparison
grammar.explanation:
Level 2 taught you far better and much worse.
Here that becomes a system with two halves.
One half says how big the gap is. The other says there is no gap at all.
grammar.rule:
How BIG the gap is, in front of the comparative:
much cheaper, far better, a lot quicker, slightly worse
considerably more expensive, nowhere near as good
NOT very cheaper. very never goes with a comparative.

NO gap, or a smaller one, with as ... as:
It is as good as the other one.        (the same)
It is not as good as the other one.    (less good)
It is not nearly as good as the other. (much less good)
It is just as good as the other one.   (exactly the same)

not as ... as is the polite way to say worse:
The second draft is not as clear.  (rather than: is worse)
grammar.workedExample:
One done, step by step.
Say this two ways: the first one costs 40, the second costs 80.
1. Using a comparative: the gap is large, so a degree word fits.
   The second one is much more expensive.
2. Using as ... as: put the cheaper one first and make it negative.
   The first one is not nearly as expensive as the second.
Both are correct. The second is softer, and that is often why you choose it.
grammar.mistake:
very cannot go in front of a comparative.
No: It is very cheaper.
Yes: It is much cheaper.
very belongs with the plain adjective: it is very cheap.
grammar.tip: much, far, a lot, slightly for the gap. as ... as when you want to be gentle about it.
grammar.practice:
Rewrite each one using not as ... as.
1. The second flat is worse than the first.
2. This route is slower than the other one.
3. The imported part is more expensive than the local one.
Now put a degree word in front of each comparative.
4. The new one is ___ cheaper. (a big gap)
5. The second draft is ___ clearer. (a small gap)
6. It is ___ more expensive than I expected. (a big gap)
7. Correct this: The metal one is very stronger.
grammar.answers:
1. The second flat is not as good as the first.
2. This route is not as fast as the other one.
3. The local part is not as expensive as the imported one.
   Note that 1, 2 and 3 all flip which thing comes first.
4. much, far or a lot  5. slightly  6. much, far or a lot
7. The metal one is much stronger. very cannot sit in front of a comparative.
5 or more right: good.

grammar.title: Learning a language takes years: -ing at the front of the sentence
grammar.explanation:
You already put -ing after a verb: I enjoy working, she stopped eating.
Here it moves to the front and becomes the SUBJECT of the sentence.
Learning a language takes years.
That is the whole increment: same form, a new place, a new job.
grammar.rule:
As the SUBJECT, at the front:
Learning a language takes years.
Waiting is the hardest part.
Getting there early made all the difference.

As the OBJECT, after the verb, which you already do:
I enjoy walking.
She avoided answering.

After a PREPOSITION, which you also already do:
I am keen on walking.
without asking, before leaving, instead of waiting

A subject -ing takes a SINGULAR verb, even with a plural after it:
Learning languages TAKES years.  (not take)

The infinitive can do the same job, and sounds more formal:
To learn a language takes years.
grammar.workedExample:
One done, step by step.
Start this sentence with an -ing word: It takes years to learn a language.
1. Find the action: to learn a language.
2. Move it to the front and change to to -ing: Learning a language.
3. That whole phrase is now the subject, and it counts as ONE thing.
4. So the verb stays singular: takes.
Answer: Learning a language takes years.
grammar.mistake:
A long -ing subject pulls people into the plural.
No: Learning languages take years.
Yes: Learning languages takes years.
The subject is the activity, which is one thing, whatever follows it.
grammar.tip: An -ing phrase at the front is one thing, so the verb is singular.
grammar.practice:
Rewrite each one so it starts with an -ing word.
1. It takes years to learn a language.
2. It is hard to wait.
3. It made all the difference to get there early.
4. It is expensive to import the parts.
Now choose the right verb.
5. Reading long reports (is / are) part of the job.
6. Learning two languages at once (is / are) difficult.
7. Finish with a preposition: I left without ___ (ask).
grammar.answers:
1. Learning a language takes years.
2. Waiting is hard.
3. Getting there early made all the difference.
4. Importing the parts is expensive.
5. is  6. is  7. asking
Numbers 5 and 6 are the trap: reports and languages are plural, but the SUBJECT
is the activity, and an activity is one thing.
5 or more right: good.

grammar.title: In charge of, under pressure, at risk: the preposition carries the meaning
grammar.explanation:
Level 2 gave you fixed phrases to learn whole: by bus, in cash, at once.
This set is different, because the preposition is doing real work.
Learn the pattern and you can build phrases you have never heard.
grammar.rule:
in  = inside a state or a role
     in charge of, in favour of, in need of, in danger, in writing

under = beneath a force acting on you
     under pressure, under review, under control, under repair

at  = a point, often a point of risk or a level
     at risk, at fault, at a loss, at short notice

on  = touching, or on behalf of
     on purpose, on behalf of, on duty, on average

out of = away from a supply or a state
     out of order, out of stock, out of date, out of work

Most take NO article:
She is in charge.  NOT in the charge.
The lift is out of order.  NOT out of the order.
grammar.workedExample:
One done, step by step.
Fill the gap: The machine is not working, so it is ___ ___ order.
1. The meaning is away from a working state.
2. Away from a state is out of.
3. These phrases take no article.
Answer: out of order.
Compare: under repair says somebody is fixing it. out of order only says it is broken.
grammar.mistake:
Adding an article breaks the phrase.
No: She is in the charge of the team.
Yes: She is in charge of the team.
in the charge of somebody means the opposite: it means they look after YOU.
grammar.tip: under = a force on you. out of = away from a state. at = a point.
grammar.practice:
Write the missing preposition. None of them takes an article.
1. She is ___ charge of the whole shift.
2. We were ___ pressure to finish by Friday.
3. The lift is ___ ___ order again.
4. Three of the houses are ___ risk.
5. I am speaking ___ behalf of the whole team.
6. The policy is ___ review at the moment.
7. He has been ___ ___ work since the factory closed.
8. Please put the request ___ writing.
grammar.answers:
1. in  2. under  3. out of  4. at  5. on  6. under  7. out of  8. in
Wrong on 3 or 7? out of means away from a state: a working state, an employed state.
Wrong on 2 or 6? under is a force acting on the thing.
6 or more right: good.

readings.title: The Auction Catalogue
readings.setting: A saleroom listing, written to be precise
readings.passage:
LOT 41. A large circular oak table, English, about 1890.
The top is in excellent condition. The legs have been repaired, and the repair is well made but visible.
Height 74cm. Diameter 140cm.

LOT 42. A pale green woollen blanket, imported, modern.
Machine-made rather than hand-woven, and not as fine as Lot 43, though considerably cheaper.
One small mark near the edge. Otherwise perfect.

LOT 43. A hand-woven woollen blanket, local, about 1950.
The colours are slightly faded. The weave is much tighter than Lot 42.
This is the better of the two, and the price reflects it.

Note for buyers. Describing a thing accurately is the whole job of a catalogue.
We do not write lovely or stunning, because those words tell you what we think and nothing about the object.
Reading a catalogue carefully saves an argument later.

readings.title: Why Very Freezing Is Wrong
readings.setting: A page from a language guide
readings.passage:
Most adjectives sit on a scale. Cold is one of them.
You can be slightly cold, quite cold, very cold or extremely cold, and each of those means something different.
A few adjectives are not on a scale at all, because they already sit at the end of one.
Freezing is the end of cold. Exhausted is the end of tired. Impossible is the end of difficult.
You cannot be very freezing, for the same reason you cannot be very finished.
There is nothing further along to point at.
What these adjectives take instead is a word that means completely: absolutely, utterly, totally.
Absolutely freezing is correct. Very freezing is not.
The mistake is common and it is worth fixing, because it is one of the few errors that native speakers notice immediately.
A useful test: if you can say slightly, the word is on a scale.
Slightly cold works. Slightly freezing does not.

readings.title: Returns and Refunds: Describe the Fault
readings.passage:
RETURNS FORM
Order number: 4471-B
Item: Two-metre steel shelving unit, flat-packed

Reason for return (tick one)
[ ] Not as described   [x] Damaged on arrival   [ ] Changed my mind   [ ] Wrong item sent

Describe the fault in your own words. Be specific: we cannot act on 'it is bad'.
One of the four uprights is bent. The bend is slight but the unit will not stand level.
The packaging was undamaged, so the part was probably bent before it was packed.

What would you like us to do?
[x] Send a replacement part   [ ] Full refund   [ ] Collection and refund

Returns are free within thirty days. After thirty days we charge for collection.
Photographs help and are not required. Do not return the whole unit unless we ask you to.

comprehension.q: Which lot is the better blanket, 42 or 43?
comprehension.why: Lot 43's entry says 'This is the better of the two'.

comprehension.q: What is wrong with the legs of the table in Lot 41?
comprehension.a: They have been repaired, and the repair can be seen.
comprehension.why: The entry says the repair is well made but visible.

comprehension.q: Why does the catalogue refuse to write words like 'lovely'?
comprehension.a: Because they say what the writer thinks, not what the object is like.
comprehension.why: The note for buyers says exactly that.

comprehension.q: The catalogue says Lot 42 is 'not as fine as Lot 43'. Say the same thing with a comparative.
comprehension.why: not as ... as reverses which item comes first, and is the gentler way to say it.

comprehension.q: What test does the article give for whether an adjective is on a scale?
comprehension.a: Try putting slightly in front of it.
comprehension.why: The last three lines: slightly cold works, slightly freezing does not.

comprehension.q: Why can you not say 'very freezing'?
comprehension.a: Freezing is already the end of the cold scale, so there is nothing further to point at.
comprehension.why: The article compares it with very finished.

comprehension.q: Which three words does the article offer instead of very, for these adjectives?
comprehension.why: Named directly, as words that mean completely.

comprehension.q: The form says 'we cannot act on it is bad'. What does the customer write instead?
comprehension.a: That one upright is slightly bent, so the unit will not stand level.
comprehension.why: The description names the part, the fault and the consequence.

comprehension.q: You want to return something forty days after it arrived. What will it cost?
comprehension.a: You will be charged for collection.
comprehension.why: Returns are free within thirty days; after that they charge.

comprehension.q: Should you send the whole shelving unit back?
comprehension.a: No, not unless they ask you to.
comprehension.why: The last line says so directly.

speaking.title: Speaking 1 — Describe an object precisely
speaking.instructions:
Pick an object near you and describe it in five sentences.
Use at least one compound adjective, one material word and one degree word.
A model, so you can hear the shape:
It is a small rectangular wooden box.
The lid is hand-painted, and the paint is slightly faded.
It is not as old as it looks.
The hinges are metal and absolutely solid.
It was made locally, as far as I know.
Tap the mic. Say your five sentences. Tap again and listen.
Check: did you use a hyphenated adjective?
Did any adjective take a degree word that suits it?
speaking.tutor: Describe the object to the tutor and ask it to name every compound adjective you used.

speaking.title: Speaking 2 — The hyphen you cannot hear
speaking.instructions:
A compound adjective takes ONE main stress, on the first part.
That is how a listener knows it is one word and not two.
Listen and repeat. The capital letters show the stress.
a WELL-made chair       (one adjective)
the chair is well MADE  (two words, stress moves)
a THREE-year contract
a PART-time job
a HAND-written label
Now say these three pairs and move the stress each time.
It is a well-made chair. The chair is well made.
She has a part-time job. She works part time.
It is a hand-written label. The label was written by hand.
Tap the mic. Say the three pairs. Tap again and listen.
Check: can you hear the stress move between the two halves of each pair?
speaking.tutor: Say the three pairs and ask the tutor whether the stress moved where it should.

speaking.title: Speaking 3 — Absolutely, or slightly?
speaking.instructions:
Say eight sentences. Put the right degree word in front of each adjective.
If the adjective is on a scale, use slightly or very.
If it is already at the end of one, use absolutely or completely.
Here are the eight adjectives, in order.
freezing, cold, exhausted, tired, impossible, difficult, furious, angry.
A model: It was absolutely freezing. It was slightly cold.
Tap the mic. Say all eight as full sentences. Tap again and listen.
Check: freezing, exhausted, impossible and furious take absolutely or completely.
Cold, tired, difficult and angry take slightly or very.
speaking.tutor: Say your eight sentences. Ask the tutor whether any pairing sounded wrong.

speaking.title: Speaking 4 — Listen: two quotations for the same job
speaking.instructions:
Tap Listen. Do not read along. Listen twice.
The first firm quoted eight hundred and said three weeks.
They are a long-established local company and everybody speaks well of them.
The second quoted five hundred and said ten days.
They are much cheaper and considerably quicker, which worried me slightly.
When I asked, it turned out the second price did not include the materials.
Once you add those, the two are not as different as they looked.
Now answer. Tap the mic and say each answer.
1. How much did the first firm quote?
2. Why did the second quotation worry the speaker?
3. What did the second price leave out?
4. What is the speaker's conclusion?
Tap again and listen to your answers.
Check: 1 eight hundred. 2 it seemed too cheap and too quick.
3 the materials. 4 the two quotations are closer than they first looked.
speaking.tutor: Retell the comparison to the tutor in three sentences, then ask which detail you left out.

speaking.title: Speaking 5 — Ask four questions to pin it down
speaking.instructions:
Somebody has offered to sell you a second-hand bicycle.
Ask four questions that make the description precise.
Ask about: age, material, condition, and what has been repaired.
Models, so you can hear the shape:
How old is it, roughly?
Is the frame steel or aluminium?
What condition are the tyres in?
Has anything been replaced or repaired?
Now write four of your own about a different object and say them.
Tap the mic. Ask your four questions. Tap again and listen.
Check: does each question ask for a FACT rather than an opinion?
A question that invites lovely or great is the wrong question.
speaking.tutor: Ask the tutor your four questions and ask which one would get the most useful answer.

speaking.title: Speaking 6 — Summarise what somebody else said
speaking.instructions:
Listen again to Speaking 4, then summarise it in your own words.
Do not repeat it sentence by sentence. Say what it amounts to.
Use at least two of: so, therefore, in other words, which means.
A model of the shape:
There were two quotations, and the second looked far better.
But it left the materials out, which means the real gap is small.
So the difference was in what was counted, not in the price.
Tap the mic. Give your summary in three or four sentences.
Tap again and listen.
Check: is your summary SHORTER than the original?
Did you add a link word that shows how the parts fit?
speaking.tutor: Give the tutor your summary and ask whether a listener would need the original.

writing.title: Writing 1 — A catalogue entry
writing.prompt:
Write a catalogue entry for an object, real or invented, in the style of Reading 1.
Give size, age, material and condition. Name one fault.
Do not use lovely, stunning or beautiful: say what the object IS.
writing.model:
LOT 12. A small rectangular metal cash box, imported, about 1970.
The paint is slightly chipped along the front edge.
The lock is original and works. The key is missing.
Height 9cm. Width 24cm.
Not as heavy as it looks, and much sturdier than the modern equivalent.
writing.criteria:
Size, age, material and condition all present.
At least one compound adjective with a hyphen.
At least one comparison using not as ... as or a degree word.
No opinion adjectives standing in for a description.
writing.support: Work through the four questions in order: how big, how old, what of, what condition.
writing.extension: Add a line comparing it with a second object, using not nearly as ... as.

writing.title: Writing 2 — Compare two things without saying which is worse
writing.prompt:
Compare two things of the same kind: two flats, two routes, two jobs.
Write six sentences. Use not as ... as at least twice.
The point of the exercise is to be accurate without being rude about either one.
writing.model:
The first flat is not as light as the second, but it is much quieter.
The second is considerably closer to the station.
The kitchen in the first is slightly bigger.
Neither is as cheap as I had hoped.
The second is not nearly as well insulated, which matters in February.
On balance the first is the better of the two.
writing.criteria:
not as ... as used at least twice.
At least two degree words in front of a comparative: much, far, slightly, considerably.
No use of very in front of a comparative.
Both things described; neither dismissed.
writing.support: List four features down the page first, then write one sentence per feature.
writing.extension: Add a seventh sentence that names the one thing you could not compare, and why.

writing.title: Writing 3 — Four sentences that start with -ing
writing.prompt:
Write four sentences about the work or study you do.
Every one must START with an -ing word as its subject.
Watch the verb: an -ing subject is one thing, so it stays singular.
writing.model:
Learning the vocabulary was easier than I expected.
Getting up at five is the part I have never got used to.
Reading long documents takes me twice as long in English.
Asking for help early saves a great deal of time later.
writing.criteria:
All four start with an -ing word.
Every main verb is singular.
At least one -ing subject is followed by a plural noun, to prove the rule.
No sentence longer than twenty words.
writing.support: Write each one as It is hard to … first, then flip it to start with the -ing word.
writing.extension: Rewrite one of the four starting with To instead, and say which sounds more formal.

writing.title: Writing 4 — Fill in the returns form
writing.prompt:
Something you bought has arrived faulty. Fill in the form from Reading 3.
The fault description is the part that matters: name the part, the fault and the consequence.
Invent the order and the item.
writing.model:
Order number: 8823-K
Item: Pale grey woollen blanket, single
Reason for return: Not as described
Describe the fault: The colour is much darker than the photograph, and the blanket is
noticeably smaller than the stated size. It measures 170cm, not 200cm.
What would you like us to do? Full refund
writing.criteria:
The fault names a part, a fault and a consequence.
At least one measurement or other specific figure.
At least one comparative with a degree word.
No opinion words doing the work of a description.
writing.support: Write the bad version first — it is wrong — then ask what, how and so what.
writing.extension: Add two sentences you would say on the phone if the form got no reply.

activities.title: Practice 1 — Build the compound adjective
activities.instructions:
Make one hyphenated adjective for each.
1. A contract that lasts three years.  a ___ contract
2. A chair that was made well.  a ___ chair
3. A label written by hand.  a ___ label
4. A job that takes the full week.  a ___ job
5. A walk of twenty minutes.  a ___ walk
6. A plan for the long term.  a ___ plan
7. A blanket woven by machine.  a ___ blanket
8. A decision taken at the last minute.  a ___ decision
activities.answers:
1. three-year  2. well-made  3. hand-written  4. full-time
5. twenty-minute  6. long-term  7. machine-woven  8. last-minute
Every one keeps the middle noun SINGULAR: three-year, twenty-minute, last-minute.
6 or more right: good.
activities.solo: Write all eight, then say each one aloud with the stress on the first half.

activities.title: Practice 2 — -ing or -ed?
activities.instructions:
Choose the right form. Four of these have no partner at all.
1. The job is very (demanding / demanded).
2. I was completely (exhausting / exhausted).
3. She is an (experiencing / experienced) driver.
4. The argument was (convincing / convinced).
5. A (concerning / concerned) neighbour rang the council.
6. The work is hard but (rewarding / rewarded).
7. Everybody (involving / involved) was paid late.
8. The film was (boring / bored) and so was I.
activities.answers:
1. demanding  2. exhausted  3. experienced  4. convincing
5. concerned  6. rewarding  7. involved  8. boring (and I was bored)
Number 8 is the Level 2 pair, with both halves in one sentence.
1, 4 and 6 have no everyday -ed partner. 3, 5 and 7 have no everyday -ing partner.
6 or more right: good.
activities.solo: Write the eight, then for each one ask: is this what the thing DOES, or how a person IS?

activities.title: Practice 3 — Two ways to say the same gap
activities.instructions:
Rewrite each sentence using not as ... as. The order of the two things will flip.
1. The second flat is worse than the first.
2. This route is slower than the other one.
3. The imported part is more expensive than the local one.
4. The modern blanket is coarser than the old one.
Now put a degree word in front of each comparative.
5. The new one is ___ cheaper. (a big gap)
6. The second draft is ___ clearer. (a small gap)
7. Correct this: The metal one is very stronger.
8. Correct this: It is more better than the first.
activities.answers:
1. The second flat is not as good as the first.
2. This route is not as fast as the other one.
3. The local part is not as expensive as the imported one.
4. The old blanket is not as coarse as the modern one.
5. much, far or a lot  6. slightly
7. The metal one is much stronger.  8. It is better than the first.
Numbers 7 and 8 are the two commonest errors: very with a comparative, and more with an -er word.
6 or more right: good.
activities.solo: Write each pair side by side and read both aloud. Decide which you would actually say.

activities.title: Practice 4 — Put the -ing at the front
activities.instructions:
Rewrite each one so it begins with an -ing word.
1. It takes years to learn a language.
2. It is hard to wait.
3. It made all the difference to get there early.
4. It is expensive to import the parts.
5. It saves time to ask for help early.
Now choose the right verb.
6. Reading long reports (is / are) part of the job.
7. Learning two languages at once (is / are) difficult.
8. Getting the measurements right (matter / matters) more than anything.
activities.answers:
1. Learning a language takes years.
2. Waiting is hard.
3. Getting there early made all the difference.
4. Importing the parts is expensive.
5. Asking for help early saves time.
6. is  7. is  8. matters
6, 7 and 8 are the whole point: the subject is the ACTIVITY, and an activity is one thing.
6 or more right: good.
activities.solo: Do the first five on paper. For 6 to 8, underline the subject before choosing the verb.

activities.title: Practice 5 — The preposition before the noun
activities.instructions:
Write the missing preposition. None of these takes an article.
1. She is ___ charge of the whole shift.
2. We were ___ pressure to finish by Friday.
3. The lift is ___ ___ order again.
4. Three of the houses are ___ risk.
5. I am speaking ___ behalf of the whole team.
6. The policy is ___ review at the moment.
7. He has been ___ ___ work since the factory closed.
8. Please put the request ___ writing.
9. The part is ___ ___ stock until March.
10. She did it ___ purpose.
activities.answers:
1. in  2. under  3. out of  4. at  5. on
6. under  7. out of  8. in  9. out of  10. on
The three out of phrases all mean away from a state: working, employed, available.
under in 2 and 6 is a force acting on the thing.
8 or more right: good.
activities.solo: Write the ten, then group them by preposition and see what each group has in common.

activities.title: Practice 6 — Turn an opinion into a description
activities.instructions:
Each line says what somebody THINKS. Rewrite it to say what the thing IS.
Invent a plausible detail where you need one.
1. It is a lovely table.
2. The blanket is horrible.
3. The flat is nice.
4. That was a terrible journey.
5. The repair is bad.
activities.answers:
There is no single right answer. Each of yours should name something checkable.
1. It is a large circular oak table in excellent condition.
2. The blanket is thin, machine-made, and much smaller than the stated size.
3. The flat is light, quiet, and a ten-minute walk from the station.
4. The journey took four hours and involved two changes.
5. The repair is visible and the joint is not level.
Check yours: could somebody argue with it? A description can be checked. An opinion cannot.
activities.solo: Write both versions side by side. Underline the checkable words in the second.

activities.title: Practice 7 — Find it in the catalogue
activities.instructions:
Answer from Reading 1 only.
1. How old is the table in Lot 41?
2. Which blanket is machine-made?
3. Which blanket has faded colours?
4. Copy one compound adjective from the text.
5. Copy the sentence that uses not as ... as.
6. Copy the sentence that starts with an -ing word as its subject.
activities.answers:
1. About 1890.
2. Lot 42.
3. Lot 43.
4. 'well made', 'machine-made' or 'hand-woven'.
5. 'not as fine as Lot 43, though considerably cheaper'.
6. 'Describing a thing accurately is the whole job of a catalogue.'
   ('Reading a catalogue carefully saves an argument later' also counts.)
5 or 6 right: good.
activities.solo: Read the catalogue with a pen and mark every adjective before you answer.

quizzes.why: The noun in a compound adjective stays singular. The number already says it is more than one.

quizzes.q: A walk that takes ten minutes is a ___ walk.
quizzes.why: Hyphen, and singular in the middle. Without the hyphen it is two separate words and not one adjective.

quizzes.q: The chair is well made. Which is right in front of the noun?
quizzes.why: The hyphen appears only in front of the noun. After the noun the two words come apart again.

quizzes.q: The job never stops and asks a great deal of you. It is ___ .
quizzes.why: It describes what the job does, so -ing. There is no everyday demanded to pair with it.
demanding has no everyday -ed partner. The other three are all standard.
very never sits in front of a comparative, and cheaper already carries the -er, so more is wrong too.

quizzes.q: Lot 43 is finer than Lot 42. Which says the same thing?
options: Lot 43 is not as fine as Lot 42.
Lot 42 is as fine as Lot 43.
Lot 42 is not as fine as Lot 43.
Lot 43 is not nearly as fine.
quizzes.a: Lot 42 is not as fine as Lot 43.
quizzes.why: not as ... as flips which item comes first. Lot 42 is the lesser one, so it goes at the front.
An -ing form can be the subject of a sentence. To learn would also work; to learning never does.

quizzes.q: Learning two languages at once ___ difficult.
quizzes.why: The subject is the activity, which is one thing, however many languages follow it.

quizzes.q: The lift is broken again. It is ___ order.
quizzes.why: out of means away from a state, here a working one. under repair would mean somebody is fixing it.

quizzes.q: She is ___ charge of the whole shift.
quizzes.why: in charge of, with no article. in THE charge of somebody means the opposite: that they look after you.
freezing is already the end of the cold scale, so it takes a word meaning completely, not one meaning to a degree.

teacherNotes.note: The plan's pattern list for this unit was adjective order, comparative adverbs and gradability. Adjective order is already taught twice (L2 U9 and L2 U20) and comparative adverbs are 7Uv.03, which the plan places in Unit 3. The cards here teach the codes actually placed: 7Ug.12 (compound and participle adjectives, degree on comparatives), 7Us.05 (gerunds as subjects) and 7Uv.02 (prepositions before nouns). The plan's pattern list has been rewritten to match.

Cards 2, 3, 4 and 5 increment Level 2: U9 'Boring or Bored', U20 'Far better, much worse', U13 'Stopped to eat, or stopped eating' with L1 U19 'Hope to go, enjoy going', and U14 'By bus, in cash, at once'. Each card names its increment in its first lines.
The plural inside a compound adjective (a three-years contract) survives well past B1 because it is logical. Point at the number rather than at the rule: the number has already said it is plural.
very + comparative is the second most common error in this unit's material. It is worth correcting every time it appears, in speech as well as writing.
The singular verb after an -ing subject fails most often when a plural noun sits between them: Learning languages take years. Have the learner underline the subject before choosing the verb.

The auction catalogue in Reading 1 is deliberately flat. Learners often try to improve it by adding adjectives of opinion, which is exactly what the text argues against. That instinct is the teaching point, not a mistake to correct quietly.
The assignment is written rather than spoken, because precision of description is demonstrated on the page. Speaking 5 and 6 carry 7Sc.02 and 7Sor.02 separately.

selfAssessment.statement: I can build an adjective out of two words and keep the middle noun singular.
I can choose between an -ing and an -ed adjective, even when there is no pair.
I can say how big a difference is, using much, far or slightly.
I can say something is not as good as something else, instead of saying it is worse.
I can start a sentence with an activity and keep the verb singular.
I can say somebody is in charge, under pressure or out of work.
I can tell a description from an opinion, and write the description.
I can ask a question that gets me a fact rather than an opinion.

assignment.title: Describe it so nobody has to ask
assignment.instructions:
Choose two objects of the same kind, real or invented, and write a description of each.
Give size, age, material and condition for both, and name at least one fault in each.
Then write four sentences comparing them. Use not as ... as at least twice, and a degree word at least twice.
Use at least three hyphenated adjectives across the whole piece, and start one sentence with an -ing word.
Finish with one sentence saying which you would choose and why.
Do not use lovely, nice, great or terrible anywhere.
